x: Indus (Ladakh) – Ganga (northern plains) – Godavari – Krishna runs strictly from north to south, the key. Ganga – Mahanadi – Godavari – Krishna is also north-to-south, so the stem is loose; Yamuna–Ganga and Narmada–Kaveri orders are not clean.

evidence: PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.21 (Indus in Ladakh)
dispute: Official key: Indus – Ganga – Godavari – Krishna. Strictly, Ganga – Mahanadi – Godavari – Krishna (option 1) is also in north-to-south order.

from_notes_src: OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Geography 04 p.5-6, p.11 (Indus rises near Bokhar Chu, Kailash range; Peninsular systems)
x: All three are true: the Himalayan systems are the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra; the main Peninsular systems are the Narmada, Tapi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri and Mahanadi; and the Indus rises on the northern slopes of the Kailash range near Lake Mansarovar (Bokhar Chu glacier).
source: OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Geography 04 p.5-6, p.11 (Indus rises near Bokhar Chu, Kailash range; Peninsular systems)

from_notes_src: PMF Physical Geography 03 p.13 (consequent rivers: Godavari, Krishna, Cauvery)
x: Rivers that follow the general slope of the land are consequent rivers; the Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri, descending from the Western Ghats to the Bay of Bengal, are PMF's examples. Subsequent streams grow along weak rock at right angles; obsequent ones flow against the slope.
source: PMF Physical Geography 03 p.13 (consequent rivers: Godavari, Krishna, Cauvery)

x: The Godavari forms the extensive Konaseema delta, splitting into the Gautami and Vasishta and then seven branches; it is the largest Peninsular river. The Narmada forms an estuary, not a delta.
source: NextGen Indian Geography - APPSC Exams 07 (Part 5) p.13 (Godavari forms extensive delta in AP); PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.35 (large lobate delta)
evidence: PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.37 (Krishna delta also one of the largest in India)

from_notes_src: PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.36 (Pranahita, the largest tributary of the Godavari)
x: The Pranhita (combined Penganga, Wardha and Wainganga) is the largest tributary of the Godavari and brings the biggest flow; Manjira, Sileru (via Sabari) and Penganga (via Pranhita) are smaller.
source: PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.36 (Pranahita, the largest tributary of the Godavari)

from_notes_src: PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.36 (Pranahita forms the Maharashtra–Telangana boundary); Rocket AP Geography p.11 (Chitravathi, Papagni – Penna)
x: The Pranhita forms the Maharashtra–Telangana boundary and joins the Godavari at Kaleshwaram in Telangana, so it does not flow in AP. Budameru (NTR district), Chitravati and Papagni (Pennar tributaries) are AP rivers.
source: PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.36 (Pranahita forms the Maharashtra–Telangana boundary); Rocket AP Geography p.11 (Chitravathi, Papagni – Penna)

from_notes_src: Rocket Indian Geography p.5 (Narmada valley between Vindhya & Satpura); PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.49
x: The Narmada flows in a rift valley between the Vindhyas (north) and Satpuras (south), so it separates the Deccan Tableland from northern India. Krishna and Godavari lie wholly within the Peninsula; the Chambal drains the Malwa to the Yamuna.
source: Rocket Indian Geography p.5 (Narmada valley between Vindhya & Satpura); PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.49

from_notes_src: Rocket Indian Geography p.2 (Damodar flows through rift valley → Hugli)
x: The Damodar flows east through the Chota Nagpur plateau in a rift valley formed by down-warping (a Gondwana trough) and joins the Hugli. Mahanadi, Son and Yamuna do not occupy rift valleys.
source: Rocket Indian Geography p.2 (Damodar flows through rift valley → Hugli)

from_notes_src: PMF Physical Geography 03 p.16 (Chambal, Damodar, Subarnarekha, Banas – superimposed drainage)
x: A superimposed river keeps a course formed on an older cover rock and cuts across the structure below; PMF lists the Chambal, Damodar, Subarnarekha and Banas. Alaknanda and Kosi are Himalayan rivers, the Godavari a consequent one.
source: PMF Physical Geography 03 p.16 (Chambal, Damodar, Subarnarekha, Banas – superimposed drainage)

from_notes_src: NextGen Indian Geography - APPSC Exams 08 (Part 6) p.1; PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.49 (rift valley between the Satpura and the Vindhyan range)
x: The Narmada flows west in a rift valley between two ranges – the Vindhyas in the north and the Satpuras in the south. Sharavati, Mahi and Sabarmati do not flow between two ranges.
source: NextGen Indian Geography - APPSC Exams 08 (Part 6) p.1; PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.49 (rift valley between the Satpura and the Vindhyan range)

from_notes_src: PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.19 (Narmada and Tapi only major west-flowing rivers)
x: The Narmada is the odd one: it flows west to the Arabian Sea. The Tungabhadra (Krishna system), Penganga (Godavari system) and Mahanadi all flow east to the Bay of Bengal.
source: PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.19 (Narmada and Tapi only major west-flowing rivers)

from_notes_src: Rocket Indian Geography p.6-7 (Kali rises near Diggi, flows west → Arabian Sea)
x: A is false: the Kali (Kalinadi) of Karnataka rises near Diggi in Uttara Kannada and flows west to the Arabian Sea near Karwar. R is true: the Deccan is higher in the west and slopes east towards the Bay of Bengal.
source: Rocket Indian Geography p.6-7 (Kali rises near Diggi, flows west → Arabian Sea)

from_notes_src: NextGen Indian Geography - APPSC Exams 07 (Part 5) p.13 (west-flowing rivers lack deltas, have long deep estuaries); OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Geography 04 p.12
x: The Mahanadi is east-flowing and builds a delta near Paradeep in Odisha, so it does not make an estuary. The Narmada, Tapi and Mandovi are west-flowing rivers that end in estuaries.
source: NextGen Indian Geography - APPSC Exams 07 (Part 5) p.13 (west-flowing rivers lack deltas, have long deep estuaries); OnlyIAS NCERT Indian Geography 04 p.12

x: Naimisaranya (Nimsar, Sitapur district, UP) lies on the left bank of the Gomati (Gomti), a plains-fed Ganga tributary. It is not on the Ganga, Yamuna or Narmada.
source: Rocket Indian Geography p.8 (Lucknow – Gomati); Naimisaranya on the Gomti – general knowledge, not checked

from_notes_src: PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.8 (Cauvery delta – South India's granary)
x: The fertile soil and ample irrigation of the Cauvery (Kaveri) delta in Tamil Nadu have made it South India's granary. The Mahanadi, Godavari and Krishna deltas are rich too but are not given this name.
source: PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.8 (Cauvery delta – South India's granary)

x: The Ikshvakus' capital Vijayapuri (Nagarjunakonda) stood on the Krishna, where their queens patronised great Buddhist stupas and viharas. The Godavari, Tungabhadra and Pennar are not the Ikshvaku centres.
source: Rocket AP Geography p.5 (Nagarjuna Sagar on the Krishna); Nagarjunakonda Buddhist remains on the Krishna – general knowledge, not checked

from_notes_src: PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.37 (Krishna right bank Tungabhadra; left bank Bhima, Musi)
x: The Gomati is a Ganga tributary (Lucknow). Musi (left bank), Tungabhadra (right bank) and Bhima (left bank) are tributaries of the Krishna.
source: PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.37 (Krishna right bank Tungabhadra; left bank Bhima, Musi)

from_notes_src: Rocket Indian Geography p.3, p.6 (Teesta, Manas Brahmaputra tributaries; Luni → Rann of Kutch)
x: The Luni is an inland river of Rajasthan lost in the Rann of Kutch. The Teesta, Manas and Dihang (the Brahmaputra's name in Arunachal) belong to the Brahmaputra system.
source: Rocket Indian Geography p.3, p.6 (Teesta, Manas Brahmaputra tributaries; Luni → Rann of Kutch)

x: The Narmada is the classic rift-valley river, flowing in a fault trough between the Vindhyas and Satpuras. The Damodar's Gondwana trough is also called a rift valley, but the question's intended answer is the Narmada; the Kosi and Godavari are not rift-valley rivers in the textbooks.
source: PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.49 (Narmada flows westwards in a rift valley); Rocket Indian Geography p.2 (Damodar rift valley)

x: The Indira Sagar dam on the Narmada (Khandwa, MP) holds the largest reservoir in India by volume of water stored; Nagarjuna Sagar on the Krishna is second. Gandhi Sagar (Chambal) and Shivaji Sagar (Koyna) are smaller.
source: PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.58 (Indira Sagar – largest reservoir in India by volume; Nagarjuna Sagar second)

from_notes_src: PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.48-49 (Subarnarekha, Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Pennar, Cauvery, Vaigai north→south)

from_notes_src: PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.44 (Pennar left bank tributaries: Jayamangali, Kunderu, Sagileru)

source: PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.44 (Pennar left bank tributaries: Jayamangali, Kunderu, Sagileru)

from_notes_src: Rocket Indian Geography p.10 (Betwa – right-bank tributary of the Yamuna); PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.53-54
x: The Betwa is a Yamuna tributary that flows north-east, so it is not west-flowing. The Periyar and Bharathapuzha (Kerala) and the Sabarmati (Gujarat) flow west to the Arabian Sea.
source: Rocket Indian Geography p.10 (Betwa – right-bank tributary of the Yamuna); PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.53-54

from_notes_src: PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.48-49 (UPSC 2002, answer a)

from_notes_src: PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.55-56 (UPSC 2004, answer a 'according to UPSC', debatable)

from_notes_src: PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.49 (UPSC 2006, answer c)

from_notes_src: PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.55 (UPSC 2010, answer d)

source: PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.54 (Periyar tributaries: Cheruthoni; Idukki HEP)

from_notes_src: Rocket Indian Geography p.14 (Narmada – Tawa); PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.49
x: The Tawa is the longest tributary of the Narmada; it rises in the Mahadeo hills and joins at Bandra Bhan (Narmadapuram).
source: Rocket Indian Geography p.14 (Narmada – Tawa); PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.49

from_notes_src: Rocket Indian Geography p.7 (Mithi origin: Vihar Lake)
x: The Mithi rises at Vihar Lake in Mumbai; Powai Lake water joins it and it falls into Mahim Bay.
source: Rocket Indian Geography p.7 (Mithi origin: Vihar Lake)

from_notes_src: Rocket Indian Geography p.5 (Narmada valley between Vindhya & Satpura)
x: The Narmada flows between the Vindhyan and Satpura ranges. The Sone, Mahi and Netravati do not.
source: Rocket Indian Geography p.5 (Narmada valley between Vindhya & Satpura)

x: The Narmada basin covers a small part of Chhattisgarh on the Maikal slopes (Kabirdham/Rajnandgaon area). Raipur and Korba lie in the Mahanadi basin and Bastar in the Godavari (Indravati) basin.
source: PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.49 (Narmada basin includes Chhattisgarh); districts – general knowledge, not checked

from_notes_src: PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.19 (steep slope, short distance, rocky topography)
x: Both true: the short, swift Western Ghats rivers flow fast over hard rock and carry little silt, so they form estuaries, not deltas – R explains A.
source: PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.19 (steep slope, short distance, rocky topography)

from_notes_src: PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.47-48 (UPSC 2009, answer d)
x: Both are false: the Kabini of Wayanad flows east, and the Narmada and Tapi flow west through MP. So neither statement is correct.
source: PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.47-48 (UPSC 2009, answer d)

from_notes_src: PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.52 (Tapti left bank: Purna); NextGen Indian Geography - APPSC Exams 08 (Part 6) p.1

source: PMF Indian Physical Geography 02 p.52 (Tapti left bank: Purna); NextGen Indian Geography - APPSC Exams 08 (Part 6) p.1

from_notes_src: Rocket Indian Geography p.3 (Majuli – river island in Brahmaputra, Assam)

source: Rocket Indian Geography p.3 (Majuli – river island in Brahmaputra, Assam)

from_notes_src: Rocket Indian Geography p.3; NextGen Indian Geography - APPSC Exams 07 (Part 5) p.12
x: The shifting channels of the Brahmaputra and its tributaries (Subansiri, Kherkutia Xuti) formed Majuli island.
source: Rocket Indian Geography p.3; NextGen Indian Geography - APPSC Exams 07 (Part 5) p.12

from_notes_src: Rocket Indian Geography p.3
x: Majuli is in Assam, in the Brahmaputra.
source: Rocket Indian Geography p.3

x: The silt laid down by the Brahmaputra's annual floods makes Majuli fertile for paddy, its main crop.

from_notes_src: Rocket Indian Geography p.2 (Bhagirathi origin: Gomukh)
x: The Bhagirathi emerges at Gomukh, the snout of the Gangotri glacier, about 18 km from Gangotri town.
source: Rocket Indian Geography p.2 (Bhagirathi origin: Gomukh)

from_notes_src: NextGen Indian Geography - APPSC Exams 07 (Part 5) p.12 (Majuli the largest riverine island globally)
x: Majuli in the Brahmaputra (Assam) is described as the largest riverine island in the world.
source: NextGen Indian Geography - APPSC Exams 07 (Part 5) p.12 (Majuli the largest riverine island globally)
